summary.name: Rethinking Task Size in SRE
summary.one_liner: A Google SRE article arguing that running fewer, bigger tasks (vertical scaling) can cut fixed per-replica costs and improve service efficiency in shared computing environments.
use_cases: Deciding how many replicas to run versus how much CPU and RAM each gets
Reducing fixed overhead such as logging and monitoring across many tasks
Planning an iterative resizing experiment for a production job
Weighing efficiency gains against latency and scheduler risks
Reclaiming unused memory and CPU from over-provisioned services
summary.what_it_does: The article explains why consolidating a job into fewer, larger tasks can reduce per-replica fixed costs such as binary size, monitoring, logging and open connections, and free headroom for other jobs. It proposes an iterative reshaping process: monitor SLO and efficiency metrics, test on a subset of tasks, resize exponentially or linearly, evaluate, then roll out region by region. It recommends efficiency metrics like QPS per CPU or service productivity, and watching for regressions in tail latency, mutex contention, and thread pool queuing during peak load. A Google case study reports a video statistics job going from 26,000 tasks of 1.9 cores to 13,000 tasks of 3.8 cores, improving efficiency about 25% (200 to 250 QPS per core).
notable: Case study: 26,000 tasks of 1.9 cores reshaped to 13,000 tasks of 3.8 cores, with about 25% efficiency gain
Describes memory reclaim of about two thirds of job capacity after resizing
Discusses risks of bigger tasks: contention, memory and network bandwidth saturation, and scheduler bin-packing delays
caveats: Bigger tasks can increase contention and tail latency and reduce scheduler packing flexibility
Trades some client-perceived latency for resource savings
Written from Google's production experience; results may not transfer to other environments
